The Pediatric Digestive Tract

Diana Sorina Feier

The chapter presents the relevant gastrointestinal diseases of the neonate, infant and older child.

Standard presenting features of the neonatal gastrointestinal disease include respiratory distress, abdominal distension, delayed passage of meconium, non-bilious vomiting, rectal bleeding, jaundice, visible defects in the anterior abdominal wall.

Most of the presented pathologies are associated with additional malformations (VACTERL): vertebral (V), anorectal anomalies (A), cardiac (C), tracheoesophageal (TE), renal (R), limb (L).

34.1. Esophageal atresia

Defifinition: Due to defective tracheoesophageal separation, a blind-ending esophageal pouch may be present, either with a fifistula to the trachea or without one.

Etiology, pathophysiology, patho-

genesis: defective differentiation of the primitive foregut into esophagus, trachea, and lung in the third to sixth week of embryonal development.

Clinical aspects: prenatal hydramnios; aspiration pneumonia. There are more types, according to the cause and presence of a tracheal fifistula.

Imaging Signs (depending on the type).

Chest, abdominal, and skeletal radiograph fifindings:

  • the abdomen is free of intestinal air where the distal fifistula is absent
  • abnormal meteorism occurs in a dis- tal fifistula
  • a distal pouch may be detectable be- cause of reflflux of air from the stomach
  • pneumonia and atelectasis may occur due to aspiration
  • associated malformations of the spi- ne and extremities may be present Fluoroscopy
  • the contrast is blindly ending and pooling in an esophageal stump
  • may show evidence of the tracheoeso- phageal fifistula ­ flfluoroscopy is particularly useful in demonstrating H­type fifistula Ultrasound (US) fifindings ­ no flfluid feeling of the stomach; ­ a reduced bowel fifilling.

Complications: Aspiration pneumonia (mortality 25%); risk of perforation from the gastric tube; esophageal stricture; recurrent fifistula.

Differential Diagnosis: Aspiration pneumonia from other causes: cystic fifibrosis, gastroesophageal reflflux.

Tips and pitfalls: diagnosis should be considered before the fifirst feeding. Late abdominal radiography (12 hours postpartum) is indicated when the distal tracheoesophageal fifistula is present to demonstrate another possible atresia. The lack of an intestinal stop when placing a gastric tube can delay the diagnosis of an H fifistula. Epiglottic passage of contrast medium can lead to misdiagnosis.

34.2. Duodenal atresia

Etiology, pathophysiology, patho-

genesis: duodenal atresia is the most common cause of congenital upper intestinal occlusion with complete duodenal obstruction due to lack of recanalization of the duodenal lumen after the sixth week of fetal life. Associated anomalies occur in most patients with duodenal atresia: Down syndrome, congenital heart diseases, components of the VACTERL.

Imaging Signs

Antenatal diagnosis: ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

Ultrasonography reveals a dilated and flfluid­fifilled stomach and duodenum (having the appearance of a flfluid double bubble image), as well as polyhydramnios in 40% of cases.

On fetal MRI, the stomach and preatretic duodenum are dilated and show liquid signal inside (hypointense on T1 weighted images and hyperintense on T2 weighted images).

Postnatal diagnosis: the condition is being considered in the presence of biliary vomiting in the fifirst hours of life, but in the case of preampular atresia, vomiting can be non-biliary. There is no meconium and no signifificant upper abdominal distension.

Abdominal radiographs show the classic “double­bubble” appearance due 34. THE PEDIATRIC DIGESTIVE TRACT l 303 to the air distension of the stomach and bottom of the duodenal sac. The rest of the abdomen is entirely radiopaque. Barium transit is helpful in case of diagnostic doubts.

34.3. Small Bowel Atresia

Epidemiology: Incidence 1:400­1500. The proximal jejunum and distal ileum are more frequently affected.

Etiology, pathophysiology, pathogenesis: Atresia is presumably a sequela of ischemia during fetal development. Multiple intestinal atresias are present in 15% of cases. Associated malformations (heart, spine) are rare. The more distal the air­flfluid levels are, the more distal is the obstruction to passage. Proximal atresia produces a “triple bubble” sign. There is no air distal to the atresia. It can be associated with prenatal volvulus or meconium ileus.

Imaging Signs

Chest and abdominal radiograph fifindings. The further distal is the atresia, the more air­flfluid levels will be present. Dilated, airfifilled proximal small bowel loops appear. Placing the infant in a head-down position for a long time allows intestinal air to move as far distally as possible. There is no air in the colon. Sequelae of aspiration may be present. Other malformations may be present.

Contrast enema fifindings. Findings include microcolon or normal caliber colon depending on the level of the atresia. Colon is better developed, the higher the atresia is and the later it occurs in fetal development.

Ultrasound fifindings. Dilation of bowel loops proximal to the stenosis; abrupt change in caliber. It may visualize other malformations and/or complications. Highly active peristalsis or alternating nor304 l VII. PARTICULARITIES OF RADIODIAGNOS mal and reversed peristalsis in the proximal bowel loops may be seen.

Complications: Meconium peritonitis after perforation (cystic appearance, calcififications) occurs in 2% of cases. Postoperative short bowel syndrome and disruption of intestinal motility. Strangulation. Anastomotic stenosis.

Differential Diagnosis: Duodenal atresia; Small bowel volvulus; Malrotation; Meconium ileus; Meconium plug syndrome; Hirschsprung disease.

Tips and Pitfalls

Diagnostic techniques should be postponed until at least 12 hours postpartum. If the abdominal fifilm is obtained too early, the atresia will appear to be more proximal than it is. Due to the absence of haustration in newborns, the small bowel is often indistinguishable from the large bowel. Air will be detected in the bowel segments distal to the atresia after rectal enema.

34.4. Hirschprung’s disease (congenital megacolon)

Defifinition: Hirschprung’s disease is a pathological entity due to the absence of parasympathetic intrinsic ganglion cells in both Auerbach’s and Meissner’s plexus in the bowel wall. The distal large bowel from the point of neuronal arrest to the anus is aganglionic.

Associated malformations: Down’s syndrome, ileal and colonic atresia, cleft palate, polydactyly, craniofacial anomalies, cardiac septal defects.

The neonatal diagnosis is made clinically based on failure to pass meconium, abdominal distension, and sometimes bilious vomiting. Diarrhea may sometimes be present (causing confusion with enterocolitis).

The diagnosis of certainty: suction or full-thickness rectal biopsy. STICS IN THE PEDIATRIC PATIENT

Imaging Signs

Abdominal radiograph: low bowel obstruction, commonly with colonic dilatation out of proportion to the small bowel; absence of rectal air.

Barium enema or water-soluble contrast me- dium enema – performed in cases without peritonitis or perforation, with the catheter tip placed just inside the rectum. The most important is the lateral view obtained during slow fifilling. In short segment diseases, the rectum will be narrow, and there will be a cone-shaped transition zone to the more proximal dilated bowel. Retention of contrast above the sigmoid colon on a delayed X­ray after 24 hours is a non­specifific sign. In total aganglionosis coli shortening of the normal caliber colon is seen, with loss of the normal redundancy of the flflexures. Sometimes a microcolon is seen.

34.5. Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC)

Defifinition: the term describes the severe form of enterocolitis that affects primarily premature infants. NEC is also seen in term infants with polycythemia, cyanotic congenital heart disease and gastroschisis.

Etiology: immaturity of the gut mucosa and immune response, sepsis, early enteral feeding, umbilical arterial and venous cannulation, maternal cocaine abuse.

The clinical picture combines the digestive syndrome (vomiting, marked abdominal distension, bloody stools) with the infectious syndrome (sepsis, toxic-septic shock).

Radiographic features: diffuse gaseous distension of both small and large bowel or isolated gastric distension. Serial radiographs will demonstrate fifixed dilatation of one or more bowel loops, thickening

(edema) and loss of distinction of the bowel walls as the disease progresses. A specifific sign of NEC on the plain radiograph is submucosal or subserosal intramural air (pneumatosis intestinalis). Portal venous air is seen in approximately 10% of cases.

Ultrasonography is more sensitive than a plain radiograph in the detection of ascites and portal venous air. Pneumatosis intestinalis may be recognized with US. The ‘circle sign’ indicates air bubbles circumferentially in the bowel wall and is seen as a continuous, echogenic ring in the cross-section.

Complications: Perforation, strictures, abscess formation, enteric fifistulas, obstruction secondary to adhesions, malabsorption, and short bowel syndrome following surgical resection.

34.6. Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (HPS)

Etiology: unknown. Age of presentation: between 4 and 6 weeks. Male­tofemale ratio 3:1.

Clinical presentation: projectile vomiting. Associated clinical fifindings: weight loss, dehydration, hypochloremic alkalosis. No imaging is required if an experienced clinician can reliably palpate the hypertrophied pylorus.

Imaging Signs

Ultrasound: an accurate method- shows the thickened hypoechoic muscle and central echogenic mucosa. The margins of the pyloric canal appear as parallel, curvilinear lines on the longitudinal view.

Tips and tricks: Pylorospasm may mimic HPS on US. The measurements vary in pylorospasm with time, which can help distinguish it from HPS. 34. THE PEDIATRIC DIGESTIVE TRACT l 305

34.7. Acute appendicitis

Acute appendicitis is the most common indication for emergency abdominal surgery in children. Imaging can help diagnose or exclude acute appendicitis as a cause of acute abdominal pain or suggest alternative diagnoses.

Imaging Signs

Plain radiographs of the abdomen: usually normal in non-perforated appendicitis. A faecolith can sometimes be present at its tip.

US: performed using a linear array high-frequency transducer. The swollen appendix is a tubular, flfluid­fifilled structure, which is not compressible and measures 6mm or more in diameter (fifigure 281). The echogenic mucosal lining may be intact or poorly defifined, indicating perforation is imminent. A peri­appendicular flfluid collection occurs with early perforation. Increased peri-appendiceal echogenicity represents inflflammation of the surrounding fat. Enlarged reactive lymph nodes are commonly seen.

Computer tomography: reserved for cases where the ultrasound examination is diffificult to perform due to bowel air. The CT appearances of acute appendicitis in children are similar to those in adults.

34.8. Intussusception

Defifinition: telescoping a bowel segment (intussusceptum) into a more distal segment (intussuscipiens). It is a typical surgical emergency in infants and young children (peak incidence between 5 and 9 months). The most common type: ileocolic intussusceptions. Ileo-ileocolic, ileo-ileal, and colo-colic are much less common.

Etiology: The majority are due to lymphoid hypertrophy, usually following 306 l VII. PARTICULARITIES OF RADIODIAGNOS

The clinical presentation: episodes of intermittent colicky pain, vomiting, ‘red currant jelly’ stools (containing blood and mucus), and a palpable abdominal mass.

Imaging signs

Supine abdominal radiograph: the presence of a soft tissue mass, distal small bowel obstruction, absence of air from the colon, diffificulty in assessing the position of the caecum, or pneumo-peritoneum.   • – distal bowel segment (intussuscipiens).

Ultrasonography: a high-frequency linear array transducer should be used for diagnosis and the possibility of spontaneous reduction. On transverse imaging, it takes the form of a ‘target’. Longitudinal imaging has a ‘sandwich’ or “trident” appearance given by the wall thickening due to edema, inflflammation, or hematoma (fifigure 282). A small amount of free intraperitoneal flfluid and enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes may be present.

Treatment options: With the surgeon’s approval, the intussusception reduction may be performed using the ultrasound transducer on the abdomen or by contrast material enema under US control. Pneumatic reduction of intussusception using air under flfluoroscopic guidance may also be used. 34. THE PEDIATRIC DIGESTIVE TRACT l 307
